doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: Current life, clinics and the band as family
summary: They divide time among teaching, clinics and gigs; new band members like Nolan 'Cat Daddy' Shaheed joined the family.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Keep moving. That’s the important part. So you divide your time now here in San Diego between teaching and going out and playing gigs, and recordings.

We’ve done clinics and things like that too. Very rewarding I’d say, again, it becomes very difficult because, you know, outside traveling hassles and things like that. But in terms of actual, once you get on the stage for performance, it’s been very — we come out, as they say, smelling like a rose. Hey, whatever we went through before, we don’t even get into it because it was worthwhile to get to this.
Did you ever have the seven year period where you are saying to yourself, I don’t know if I can keep doing this?

Not yet. I think I’m not too sure, I think we’re very fortunate, and I’m not quite sure why. But so far, so good. And I think because both of us are relatively healthy and even with the advent of the new musicians, they’ve been with us now three years at least, but they’ve fell into the family mode that we love, that we had with Curtis and Red Callender. In fact Cat Daddy told, me, that’s Cat Daddy, we call him Cat Daddy—

He said, “Whenever I get on this band” he says. “I used to say why are those people asking me how I feel?” He couldn’t figure that out. Because although he was the first trumpet player for, lead trumpet player for Count Basie for a while, even at a young age, he had also played with a couple of rock & roll people, and they paid him a great salary and everything, but they just come and do what they’re doing and everybody splits. So he wasn’t quite used to that way, but it’s a family in the group. And gradually these young ones have come into the family, and the way of taking care of each other. © Fillius Jazz Archive -33-
First they’ll call up, hey how are you feeling?
Turn it around and send it back.
Then we got a gig, and everybody’s hugging. “Hey, how you doing, how you feeling?” They hug you and they know how you feel.
So it’s wonderful, I think our second family is just as nice as it was.
It’s like a blessing in a way.
Because we’re very, very, very fortunate.
